Six seeded mutations via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: 4 caught (solver uses writing hours only; revision hours rounds+perRound; floor < -> <=; blank speed defaulted to 1000), 2 survived (non-writing-share threshold >= 0.25 -> > 0.25 at calc.mjs:145; tie tolerance 0.005 -> 0.5 $/h at calc.mjs:108, so a 49-cent/h difference would be called a tie). evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (194 lines, pure, one exported function), index.html module script (lines 175-273), usage.mjs. Clean and small; innerHTML only interpolates numbers and fixed strings, no user text, so no injection path. Defects: silent fallbacks everywhere (num()/numOrZero() turn negative, NaN and blank to 0; the page also does Number(v)||0), so a typo'd field changes the answer with no message; writing speed 0 with words > 0 is accepted as zero writing hours; money() uses toLocaleString(undefined) with maximumFractionDigits 2, which is locale-dependent and wrong for per-word rates; the low-rate title says 'at or below' but the test is strict <, so $0.10 exactly is not flagged; the non-writing finding is unconditional on the comparison it sits next to.
evidence.claims: Disclaimer, no-warranty and no-upload privacy present on both pages; DNT/GPC/opt-out backed by usage.mjs. The headline claim is not backed: index.html:56 and README say the tool shows 'which one actually pays more, not just which headline number looks bigger', but for one job both prices divide by the same hours, so the verdict equals 'the bigger total' in 144 of 144 grid cases (check.mjs) and the venture's own comparison page FAQ concedes 'For the SAME job, yes -- the higher total dollar amount and the higher effective hourly rate always agree'. The FAQ (index.html:150, JSON-LD) says that with heavy research 'a flat fee usually pays a higher effective hourly rate than an equivalent per-word rate'; research hours cannot change which option wins, and 'equivalent' is undefined. Rate bands checked against bestwriting.com's 2026 pages (via WebSearch; bestwriting.com and the-efa.org do not resolve from this session): $0.42 average from 500 writers January 2026 and $0.70 AWAI copywriter figure are attributed consistently; but bestwriting's own tiers put beginners at $0.15/word and say 50.6% of writers earn below $0.10, so '$0.05-$0.10 entry level' that 'every 2026 rate guide above agrees on' (calc.mjs:60) is not what the cited source says. Ghostwriting: the 16-20% premium is from one Peak Freelance survey of 213 writers (36% of ghostwriters charge extra; the 16-20% 'majority' is the intro's framing, the body says almost half add at least 16%, income data from 2020); calc.mjs:26 'multiple 2026 rate-guide sources agree' and the page's 'per 2026 rate-guide surveys' overstate it. Canonical in index.html points at duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects, which build_pages_site.py rewrite_base_urls (line 110 pattern includes /monorepo-projects) rewrites at deploy: source-only.
evidence.fitness: Walked a writer's job: a client offers $0.20/word or $500 for a 1,500-word researched piece. The tool tells them $500 is better (obvious from the totals) and that $675 hits $75/h, which is the one genuinely useful output. What the professional actually needs to decide is not modelled: what a third or fourth revision round costs under each price (per-word gets nothing, flat gets nothing unless an overage rate is set), what happens if the piece runs 2,000 words (per-word pays for it, flat does not), a kill fee, platform cut, self-employment tax and unbillable hours (pitching, invoicing) that make a gross $75/h a much lower take-home. No way to start from an annual income target. The contradictory 25% finding could push a writer toward the lower-paying option.
evidence.domain: Compared against common freelance pricing practice (Peak Freelance 2026 rates guide and bestwriting.com 2026 rates, via search; EFA rate chart's hourly-plus-estimate framing). Right: converting any price to an effective hourly over all hours, including research and revisions, and solving the fee for a target hourly, is the standard project-pricing method. Departures: the framing that 'a per-word rate does not compensate research' while a flat fee does is wrong as economics (a per-word rate a pro sets already prices research; for a given offer, both are fixed sums over the same hours); the real per-word vs flat difference is risk allocation (length overrun, extra rounds, scope creep), which the tool ignores; no out-of-scope revision rate or contingency buffer, which pricing guides recommend; target hourly is gross with no SE tax (15.3% on 92.35%) or overhead (stated limit).

defects.what: The page's core promise, 'which one actually pays more, not just which headline number looks bigger', is not something the tool does: for one job both prices divide by the same hours, so the verdict always equals the bigger total (144 of 144 grid cases), as the venture's own comparison page FAQ admits. The index FAQ adds that with heavy research a flat fee 'usually pays a higher effective hourly rate than an equivalent per-word rate', which hours cannot cause.

The >=25% non-writing finding tells the user a flat fee 'typically pays a higher effective hourly rate than the same per-word rate' even when the tool has just said the per-word rate pays more ($0.50/word vs $400 flat: 'per-word pays $38.89/hr more' plus the contrary finding).

A blank or zero writing speed with a nonzero word count silently drops all writing time and still shows hourly rates and a verdict (1,500 words, speed blank: 6 h, $50/h, '100% research and revisions').
Two seeded mutations survive 41 tests: the 25% non-writing threshold boundary and the tie tolerance (0.005 -> 0.5 $/h); no test checks findings against betterOption or blank speed with words.

No out-of-scope revision rate, length overrun, kill fee or contingency: the risks that actually separate per-word from flat pricing are not modelled; the hourly is gross of self-employment tax (14.13% of net) and unbillable time.

Rate-band and ghostwriting claims overstate their sources: '$0.05-$0.10 entry level ... every 2026 rate guide agrees' vs bestwriting's own $0.15 beginner tier; '16-20% ... multiple 2026 rate-guide sources agree' is one 213-writer Peak Freelance survey.

money() rounds per-word rates to cents and drops trailing zeros: a solved $0.0125/word shows as '$0.01/word' (20% low), $0.10 as '$0.1/word'; uses toLocaleString(undefined), so output varies by locale.
Canonical link points at duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects; build_pages_site.py rewrites it at deploy.

verdict: The arithmetic is right: every figure I recomputed by hand (9 h, $33.33/h, $55.56/h, $675 or $0.45/word for $75/h, the page defaults) matches. But the product's premise does not hold: for a single job both prices are divided by the same hours, so the 'which pays more per hour' verdict is always the bigger headline total, which its own comparison page concedes, while the main page and FAQ promise more. One finding gives advice that contradicts the verdict next to it, a blank writing speed silently yields wrong hourly rates, the solver rounds sub-cent per-word rates, two of six seeded mutations survive 41 tests, and the cited rate bands and ghostwriting premium are stated more strongly than their sources. The useful part is the target-hourly solver. It does not meet the bar: claims 1; correctness, verification, craft, fitness and domain 2; completeness 3.
